subChunks.title: Work, Organisations & Human Performance
subChunks.hookHtml: In 2021, Microsoft surveyed 30,000 workers across 31 countries and found that 41% were considering quitting their jobs — a figure that would materialise as the 'Great Resignation', one of the most significant labour market shifts in decades. Behind that statistic were questions that psychologists had been studying for over a century: Why are some people deeply engaged at work while others are chronically disengaged? What makes leadership effective or destructive? Why do some teams achieve extraordinary things while others collapse in conflict? How can organisations select, develop, and retain people whose contribution is genuinely valuable — not just visible? Occupational and organisational (O/O) psychology applies psychological theory and methods to the world of work: understanding human behaviour in organisational contexts, measuring performance and wellbeing, and designing conditions in which both individuals and organisations can function effectively. It is one of the largest applied psychology specialisms in the UK, and its methods — from psychometric selection to organisational interventions — touch most working adults' lives whether they know it or not.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Field and Its Scope

Occupational and organisational psychology (called Industrial-Organisational or I-O psychology in the US) spans two interrelated domains:

Occupational (individual level)   — selection, assessment, training,
                                    performance management, career
                                    development, occupational health

Organisational (group/system level) — leadership, team dynamics, culture,
                                      change management, job design,
                                      organisational development

The British Psychological Society (BPS) Division of Occupational Psychology (DOP) and the CIPD (Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development) jointly define the field's professional standards in the UK. In the US, the Society for Industrial and Organizational Psychology (SIOP) performs the equivalent function. The field is distinctively scientist-practitioner in orientation: O/O psychologists are expected to apply empirical methods, not just intuition or conventional management wisdom.

Personnel Selection: Validity and Assessment

One of the most practically important contributions of O/O psychology is the development of rigorous, valid personnel selection methods. The central question: which selection methods best predict job performance?

Schmidt and Hunter's (1998) meta-analysis of 85 years of selection research is one of the most cited findings in all of applied psychology. Key validity coefficients (correlation with job performance):

Work sample tests              r = .54   — doing the job task itself
Cognitive ability tests        r = .51   — general mental ability (GMA/g)
Structured interviews          r = .51   — standardised questions, anchor scores
Integrity tests                r = .41   — honesty/conscientiousness measures
Assessment centres             r = .37   — multi-method, multi-assessor
Biodata                        r = .35   — systematic biographical information
Unstructured interviews        r = .38   — but highly variable; subject to bias
Years of education             r = .10   — weak predictor
Age                            r = -.01  — essentially zero

Cognitive ability (GMA) is the single strongest individual predictor across almost all jobs. It predicts learning rate, problem-solving, and adaptability. However, GMA tests show adverse impact — systematically lower mean scores for some racial/ethnic minority groups — creating legal and ethical tensions between validity and fairness in selection. Structured interviews, personality assessments (particularly Conscientiousness), and integrity tests can supplement GMA while reducing adverse impact.

Personality in selection: The Big Five framework dominates personality-based selection research. Conscientiousness (r ≈ .22–.31 with job performance across studies) is the most consistent Big Five predictor, followed by Emotional Stability (particularly for stress-prone roles). Faking and socially desirable responding remain challenges for self-report personality measures in high-stakes selection contexts.

Job Satisfaction, Engagement and Motivation at Work

Job satisfaction is the degree to which an employee has a positive evaluation of their job. It is multidimensional: facet satisfaction (pay, colleagues, task variety, supervision, opportunities) and global satisfaction. Job satisfaction predicts attendance, retention, and customer satisfaction but shows only modest correlations with individual performance (r ≈ .30) — the 'happy-productive worker' hypothesis is supported but not as strongly as managerial intuition suggests.

Employee engagement — defined by Schaufeli et al. (2002) as a positive, fulfilling, work-related state characterised by vigour, dedication, and absorption — is more strongly performance-related than satisfaction. Engaged employees invest discretionary effort, are more innovative, and are less likely to leave.

Key motivation theories:

  • Herzberg's two-factor theory: Hygiene factors (pay, working conditions, job security) prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate. Motivators (achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, growth) produce genuine motivation. Practical implication: improving hygiene factors alone will not increase performance — motivators must be built into job design.
  • Hackman & Oldham's Job Characteristics Model (1976): Five core job characteristics — skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy, and feedback — interact to produce experienced meaningfulness, responsibility, and knowledge of results, leading to intrinsic motivation, satisfaction, and low absenteeism. The model underpins job enrichment as an intervention: redesigning jobs to increase these characteristics.
  • Self-Determination Theory (Ryan & Deci, 2000): Distinguishes autonomous motivation (intrinsic, integrated) from controlled motivation (external reward, introjection). Environments that support basic psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness produce autonomous motivation, which predicts performance quality, wellbeing, and persistence more reliably than extrinsic incentives.

Leadership: Theories and Evidence

Leadership research has generated more published studies than almost any other topic in organisational behaviour. Key frameworks:

Transactional leadership involves an exchange relationship: followers receive rewards (pay, promotion, recognition) in return for performance. Transactional approaches motivate compliance but not innovation or discretionary effort.

Transformational leadership (Bass, 1985) involves inspiring followers to transcend self-interest for collective goals through: Idealised Influence (being a role model), Inspirational Motivation, Intellectual Stimulation (challenging assumptions), and Individualised Consideration (attending to each follower's needs). Meta-analyses consistently show transformational leadership has stronger effects on follower satisfaction, motivation, and team performance than transactional approaches.

Authentic leadership emphasises self-awareness, transparent values, and relational openness — leaders who know themselves and behave consistently. Research links authentic leadership to trust and follower wellbeing.

Toxic leadership is increasingly studied: leaders who use intimidation, humiliation, or political manipulation to achieve goals. Toxic leadership predicts follower burnout, psychological harm, and organisational dysfunction. Narcissistic personality features in leaders are associated with short-term charisma but long-term organisational damage.

Occupational Stress and Wellbeing

The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) estimates that work-related stress, depression, and anxiety account for over 50% of working days lost in the UK. O/O psychologists use several frameworks to understand and intervene:

Karasek's Demand-Control Model: High job demands + low decision latitude ('job strain') predicts poor health outcomes. High demand + high control ('active jobs') can promote learning and engagement. Social support modifies this relationship.

Effort-Reward Imbalance (Siegrist, 1996): Imbalance between effort invested and rewards received (pay, esteem, promotion) predicts cardiovascular and mental health risks.

The Conservation of Resources (COR) theory (Hobfoll): Stress occurs when resources (material, social, energy, identity) are threatened, lost, or when investments fail to generate expected returns. Resource loss is more impactful than resource gain — organisations that drain resources without replenishing them produce chronic stress.

Interventions are classified as primary (job redesign, workload management), secondary (resilience training, stress management skills), or tertiary (EAP counselling, return-to-work support). Research supports primary interventions as most effective — changing the stressor — with secondary and tertiary interventions providing support but not addressing root causes.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen opens the session with a question: 'Think of the best and worst manager you've ever had. What specifically made the difference?' The room is animated — this one is personal.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: Every answer you just gave me — and I've heard dozens of them over the years — maps onto decades of leadership research. Respect, clarity, being listened to, trust, being given room to grow — these come up every time. What we know empirically lines up with what people know intuitively. The gap is that organisations keep promoting people who are technically excellent into management roles and then being surprised when it goes wrong. Occupational psychology says: leadership is a set of behaviours that can be assessed, developed, and evaluated — not a personality trait some people have and others don't.

storyBeats.speaker: The validity of selection methods
storyBeats.text: In 2019, a major UK retailer replaced its unstructured 'culture fit' interviews with a structured situational judgement test and a cognitive ability measure, based on O/O psychologist recommendations. Eighteen months later, first-year retention had increased by 22% and performance ratings for new hires were significantly higher than under the previous process. The unstructured interviews had been selecting for social similarity — candidates who felt 'familiar' to interviewers — rather than job-relevant competence. This is exactly what Schmidt and Hunter's meta-analysis predicted: unstructured interviews, despite feeling rich and interpersonally valid to interviewers, are poor predictors of performance precisely because they are dominated by irrelevant social impressions.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: The research on job enrichment has a quietly radical implication. Most people's jobs are not intrinsically motivating by design — they were designed for efficiency, division of labour, cost control. When organisations discover that motivated people perform better, they often reach for extrinsic incentives first: bonuses, reward schemes. Hackman and Oldham's model says: the most powerful levers are in the job itself. Autonomy, feedback, variety, significance. Those cost nothing — except the willingness to share control.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
A large financial services organisation approaches an occupational psychologist with two concerns. First, they are experiencing high turnover among newly hired analysts (average tenure: 14 months), and their hiring managers complain that the current selection process — which uses an unstructured panel interview plus a degree grade requirement — 'isn't finding the right people.' Second, a recent employee engagement survey found that only 34% of staff described themselves as 'highly engaged', with the main themes being lack of autonomy, unclear performance feedback, and feeling that their work 'doesn't make a difference.'

  1. Recommend two evidence-based changes to the selection process, drawing on Schmidt and Hunter's validity findings. Explain why each change is likely to improve selection quality.
  2. Using Hackman and Oldham's Job Characteristics Model, identify three specific job redesign interventions that could address the engagement themes identified in the survey.
  3. The HR director suggests the engagement problem could be solved by introducing a bonus scheme. What does the psychological evidence say about the likely effectiveness of this approach, and what should the psychologist advise?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Two evidence-based selection changes: (a) Replace the unstructured panel interview with a structured interview. Structured interviews (r = .51 with job performance; Schmidt & Hunter, 1998) dramatically outperform unstructured interviews (r = .38 with high variance) because standardised questions with behaviourally anchored rating scales reduce the influence of irrelevant social impressions and interviewer bias. Each candidate is asked the same questions and rated against pre-defined criteria, making comparisons fairer and more predictive. (b) Add a cognitive ability (GMA) test. General mental ability is among the strongest individual predictors of job performance across most roles (r = .51). For analytical roles requiring problem-solving, learning, and adaptability, GMA tests provide incremental validity over interview data alone. Note: the psychologist should also advise monitoring for adverse impact and considering structured interview and GMA score weighting to balance validity and fairness.

2. Three job redesign interventions from the JCM: (a) Autonomy — the survey finding of 'lack of autonomy' maps directly to the JCM's autonomy dimension. Intervention: give analysts ownership of defined client relationships or project streams, with responsibility for planning their own workflow rather than following a prescribed task list. Research shows autonomy is the strongest single JCM predictor of intrinsic motivation. (b) Feedback — build structured, specific performance feedback into the work itself (not just annual appraisals): for example, real-time data dashboards showing individual contribution to outcomes, or regular brief structured feedback conversations with supervisors tied to specific observable work outputs. Feedback from the job itself is more intrinsically motivating than feedback delivered externally. (c) Task significance — the theme of work 'not making a difference' reflects low task significance. Intervention: connect analysts directly to end-user outcomes — e.g., client presentations, exposure to how their analysis is used in strategic decisions. Making the downstream impact of the work visible increases experienced meaningfulness.

3. The bonus scheme advice: Extrinsic financial incentives (bonuses) are unlikely to solve a fundamental engagement problem rooted in job design. Self-Determination Theory (Ryan & Deci, 2000) predicts that introducing extrinsic rewards for activities that have low intrinsic motivation will not produce durable engagement — and may undermine intrinsic motivation if it exists (the 'overjustification effect'). Research consistently shows that for complex, cognitively demanding work, financial incentives beyond a threshold of perceived fairness do not reliably increase performance quality or engagement. Herzberg's two-factor theory makes a similar prediction: pay is a hygiene factor that prevents dissatisfaction but does not produce genuine motivation. The psychologist should advise that the bonus scheme may reduce short-term dissatisfaction about pay fairness but will not address the identified root causes (autonomy, feedback, significance), and recommend prioritising job redesign interventions. Bonuses can appropriately recognise performance outcomes once intrinsic motivation is restored, but should not be the primary engagement strategy.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: A colleague argues that personality testing in recruitment should be banned because personality traits cannot be changed and using them in selection amounts to discrimination based on stable characteristics unrelated to effort or merit. Critically evaluate this argument, drawing on evidence for the validity and limitations of personality assessment in selection contexts. Aim for 200–250 words.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
The argument raises legitimate ethical concerns but contains important inaccuracies. Personality traits — particularly Conscientiousness, Emotional Stability, and Agreeableness — do show meaningful validity for predicting job performance, particularly for roles requiring reliability, stress tolerance, and interpersonal skill. Meta-analyses find Conscientiousness r ≈ .22–.31 with job performance across diverse roles, and these relationships appear robust and theoretically coherent — Conscientiousness reflects goal-directed effort, organisation, and dependability, which are clearly relevant to sustained performance.

However, the argument contains a philosophically important challenge. If personality traits are stable and heritable, selection based on personality privileges innate characteristics over effort or acquired skills — raising fairness concerns, particularly where traits are differentially distributed across demographic groups. Research does find mean-level group differences on some Big Five dimensions, though effect sizes are generally smaller than for cognitive ability tests.

The colleague is also incorrect that traits cannot change. Longitudinal research (Roberts et al., 2006) consistently shows personality development across adulthood — Conscientiousness and Agreeableness typically increase with age and work experience — challenging the assumption that personality selection simply screens for fixed, unmodifiable characteristics.

The most defensible position is: personality assessment has genuine, if modest, validity when used as one component of a multi-method selection process — supplementing rather than replacing cognitive and situational assessment. Prohibition would be an overcorrection; the appropriate responses are rigorous validation, transparency, and monitoring for adverse impact. Blanket bans on evidence-based selection methods do not serve candidates or organisations well.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old why most job interviews are poor at predicting whether someone will be good at the job — and what psychologists have found actually works better.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The 'g factor' — a general cognitive capacity that underpins performance on diverse mental tasks. The strongest individual predictor of job performance across most roles, accounting for learning speed, problem-solving, and adaptability.

When a selection method produces systematically lower pass rates for members of a protected group (e.g., race, sex) relative to the majority group, even when the method is job-relevant. Creates legal and ethical tensions in selection design.

Redesigning jobs to increase intrinsic motivation by adding the five core characteristics in Hackman and Oldham's model: skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy, and feedback from the job itself.

Bass's (1985) model of leadership based on inspiring followers to transcend self-interest through Idealised Influence, Inspirational Motivation, Intellectual Stimulation, and Individualised Consideration. Consistently outperforms transactional leadership in meta-analyses.

questions.questionHtml: According to Schmidt and Hunter's (1998) meta-analysis, which two selection methods are among the strongest predictors of job performance?
options: Unstructured interviews and years of relevant experience
Work sample tests and cognitive ability tests
questions.correctAnswer: Work sample tests and cognitive ability tests
questions.explanationHtml: Schmidt and Hunter's landmark meta-analysis of 85 years of selection research found work sample tests (r = .54) and cognitive ability tests (r = .51) among the strongest predictors of job performance. Structured interviews also showed strong validity (r = .51). Unstructured interviews, years of experience, and educational qualifications showed substantially weaker validity, often heavily influenced by irrelevant factors such as interviewer liking or prestige of educational institution rather than job-relevant capability.

questions.questionHtml: True or False: According to Herzberg's two-factor theory, improving pay and working conditions is the most effective way to increase employee motivation and performance.
questions.explanationHtml: False. Herzberg's two-factor theory distinguishes hygiene factors (pay, physical working conditions, job security, company policy) from motivators (achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, growth). Hygiene factors, when inadequate, produce dissatisfaction — but when adequate, they merely prevent dissatisfaction; they do not produce positive motivation. Only motivators — factors intrinsic to the work itself — produce genuine motivation and performance enhancement. This counterintuitive finding has been replicated across many workplace studies and underpins the case for job enrichment over purely economic incentive approaches.

questions.questionHtml: A manager argues that personality testing in selection should be abandoned because 'you can't change your personality, so it's just discrimination.' Which response most accurately evaluates this claim?
options: Correct — personality is fully fixed and therefore irrelevant to selection

Personality shows modest but consistent validity for predicting job performance, particularly Conscientiousness, and longitudinal research shows personality traits do change across adulthood; appropriate use with adverse impact monitoring is more defensible than abolition
Incorrect — personality is far more predictive than cognitive ability and should be the primary selection tool
Correct — all selection methods that correlate with stable individual differences constitute unlawful discrimination
questions.correctAnswer: Personality shows modest but consistent validity for predicting job performance, particularly Conscientiousness, and longitudinal research shows personality traits do change across adulthood; appropriate use with adverse impact monitoring is more defensible than abolition
questions.explanationHtml: Personality tests — particularly measures of Conscientiousness — show genuine, if modest, validity for predicting job performance (r ≈ .22–.31 for Conscientiousness across meta-analyses). The claim that personality is immutable is inconsistent with longitudinal research (Roberts et al., 2006) showing mean-level personality development across adulthood. The argument also confuses selection based on job-relevant characteristics with discrimination — the defining feature of unlawful discrimination is adverse treatment based on protected characteristics (race, sex, disability, etc.), not use of any characteristic that varies between people. Appropriate responses to limitations of personality assessment include using it as one component of multi-method selection, validating for specific roles, and monitoring for adverse impact — not abolition of an evidence-based method.
